tagline: Shortgrass prairie, eroded buttes and a railroad town’s second start
intro: Pawnee Pioneer Trails crosses the Colorado Piedmont on a route that includes unpaved county roads. The Colorado Department of Transportation gives the drive as 128 miles and three hours, highlighting the Pawnee Buttes and shortgrass prairie habitat for pronghorn, prairie dogs and birds. It is a Colorado Scenic and Historic Byway through Logan, Morgan and Weld counties.

Railroads helped establish towns along this landscape: the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy platted Raymer in 1888. Raymer’s first post office closed in 1895 as families moved away. Replatting in 1909 brought the community a second start and a post office with a new name, New Raymer. Keota became a station on the Burlington & Missouri River Railroad’s Old Prairie Dog Express, and water was brought to town in rail cars. Limited farming in the early 20th century ended on land now within Pawnee National Grassland after the Dust Bowl.

Begin at Ault’s junction of US 85 and Highway 14, then reach Briggsdale at the grassland’s southern end. Grover lies between the grassland’s two parcels near Crow Creek; the Pawnee Buttes rise in the eastern prairie. Continue to Raymer, whose railroad-platted townsite dates to 1888. Fort Morgan and Sterling are further byway anchors, with museums featured by CDOT.

moments.title: Grover
moments.text: Grover lies near Crow Creek, directly between the two large parcels of Pawnee National Grassland. It also has a place in fiction: Willa Cather’s 1900 short story The Affair at Grover Station describes a red station, coal sheds and a small group of dwellings. Her phrase “at the end of everything” belongs to that literary portrait. The town recorded 157 residents in the 2020 census, a 14.60 percent increase since 2010.

moments.title: Pawnee Buttes
moments.text: The Pawnee Buttes rise approximately 300 feet above the surrounding plains, remnants left as the High Plains surface wore away. Their lower layers are soft, clay-rich rock; harder sandstone and conglomerate protect the tops from weathering. Blue grama and buffalo grass dominate the shortgrass prairie surrounding them. A trail provides foot access, but ownership differs between the pair: the west butte is within the national grassland and the east butte is on private land. On protected north-facing cliff edges and in narrow canyons, scarp woodlands include limber pine, small ponderosa pines and Rocky Mountain juniper.

moments.title: Raymer
moments.text: Raymer and New Raymer are two official names for the same community, preserving two chapters of its history. The Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad platted it in 1888 and named it for assistant chief engineer George Raymer. Families later moved away, and the post office closed in 1895. Replatting in 1909 brought a new post office called New Raymer to distinguish it from the old one. When incorporation followed in 1919, the town kept the original name, Raymer. Colorado uses Raymer, while the Postal Service uses New Raymer; maps can carry either name for the town.
